title: Neuroimaging methods: fMRI, EEG and MEG
stage: College neuroscience and cognitive science degree
audience: a college student in a neuroscience, cognitive science, psychology or biology degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Learn how brain-imaging data are produced and analyzed, in Python: the physics of MRI and the BOLD signal, the hemodynamic response, experimental designs for fMRI, preprocessing, the general linear model, contrasts and statistical maps, multiple comparisons and cluster inference, region-of-interest and multivariate pattern analysis, functional connectivity, EEG and MEG signals, event-related potentials and time–frequency analysis, and the common pitfalls of circular analysis and reverse inference.
primary_reading: Andy's Brain Book, a free online guide to neuroimaging analysis

weeks.1: MRI physics in outline and the BOLD signal
weeks.4: Preprocessing: motion, slice timing, registration and smoothing
weeks.5: The general linear model for fMRI
weeks.8: Regions of interest and circular analysis
weeks.12: Time–frequency analysis and source localization in outline

blocks.deliverable: Convolve a supplied event sequence with a hemodynamic response.
Compare a block and an event-related design for a question.
Fit a general linear model to a short time series in code.
Week 7 midterm; correct a supplied set of voxel tests.
Decode a condition from supplied voxel patterns with cross-validation.
Compute an event-related potential from supplied trials.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Imaging analysis: analyze a small supplied fMRI-like data set (a few regions, a design and time series) and a small EEG-like data set in plain Python written without imaging libraries for the core steps, fitting a general linear model with contrasts and computing an event-related potential, and write a methods and results section that reports corrections, effect sizes and limitations correctly.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
